title: Borealis Geopower Inc. (Sept 2018 TCC) SR&ED Decision
subject: Geothermal energy company SR&ED appeal assessing whether resource exploration and engineering work qualified for credits.
summary: Borealis Geopower Inc. v. The Queen, 2018 TCC 189, shows Canadian corporations claiming SR&ED tax credits that government assistance is "received" when a cheque is deposited into an account the taxpayer controls. The Tax Court held that a $528,560 SDTC advance placed in a self-styled trust account reduced the 2014 SR&ED expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(d).
metaDescription: Review the September 2018 Tax Court of Canada decision for Borealis Geopower Inc. concerning Canadian SR&ED tax credit regulations.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Borealis Geopower Inc. v. Her Majesty The Queen, 2018 TCC 189 (Docket: 2017-3210(IT)I), delivered by Justice Diane Campbell on September 13, 2018, following an oral hearing in Calgary, Alberta on June 22, 2018, stands as an instructive Canadian judicial illustration—though, as a decision rendered under the Tax Court's informal procedure (Docket suffix "(IT)I"), it is not to be treated as a precedent for any other case pursuant to section 18.28 of the Tax Court of Canada Act—of the statutory timing of government assistance within the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive regime. While a substantial body of Canadian SR&ED litigation centres on whether a taxpayer's technical operations satisfy the scientific eligibility criteria of subsection 248(1) of the federal Income Tax Act (the "Act"), Borealis Geopower addresses an equally decisive fiscal vulnerability: the statutory reduction of otherwise eligible SR&ED expenditure pools and the clawback of Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) triggered by the receipt of public funding.
The Taxpayer's Operations and Claim

Borealis Geopower Inc. (the "Appellant"), represented by counsel Melanie Pituch, operates as a privately owned Canadian corporation engaged in geothermal power exploration, development, and utilization within Canada. To finance its geothermal development initiatives, the Appellant entered into a Contribution Agreement with Sustainable Development Technology Canada ("SDTC"), a foundation established by the Government of Canada to fund and support clean technology projects. The Contribution Agreement set out the contractual terms, project milestones, and conditions governing SDTC's financial contributions toward the Appellant's eligible project costs.

In August 2014, the Appellant received a cheque from SDTC in the amount of $528,560.00 representing the first advance of the project contribution under the Contribution Agreement. Upon receiving the cheque in 2014, the Appellant deposited the $528,560.00 into a separate bank account established at the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce ("CIBC"), which the Appellant designated internally as a "trust account". As testified on cross-examination by Mr. Timothy Thompson, the current Chairman of Borealis Geopower Inc., the SDTC funds were left in this separate CIBC account "until such a time as we were allowed to withdraw"; on re-direct, he further testified that withdrawals were made as the work continued and that some money was redeposited at year end because of overdraws.

On December 23, 2015, the Appellant late-filed its corporate income tax return for the 2014 taxation year, which was due on July 2, 2015, continuing a pattern of delayed compliance that had previously seen its income tax returns for the 2011 and 2013 taxation years—due on July 3, 2012, and July 2, 2014, respectively—filed late on June 30, 2015. In its 2014 return, the Appellant reported net taxable income of over $91,000.00, claimed the SR&ED ITC, and filed an SR&ED Expenditures Claim Form, resulting in no tax owing as filed due to the tax credit. Crucially, the Appellant did not include the $528,560.00 advanced by SDTC in its 2014 income tax return, taking the position that the SDTC funds were neither received nor entitled to be received in 2014 because they were held in a trust account. The Appellant maintained that because the funds were voluntarily deposited into a trust account and remained subject to unfulfilled conditions in 2014, the corporation had not legally "received" the SDTC funds in the 2014 taxation year.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Following an audit review of the Appellant's claim, the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister"), represented at the hearing by respondent counsel Peter Basta, accepted that the project met the definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the Act and accepted the Appellant's SR&ED expenditures of approximately $373,000.00. However, the Minister challenged the taxation year in which the SDTC funding was recognized for purposes of the SR&ED expenditure pool and ITC calculations. By an assessment dated August 12, 2016, the Minister assessed the Appellant's 2014 taxation year on the basis that the Appellant had received government assistance of $528,560.00 from SDTC in the 2014 taxation year.

The Minister's assessment rested on the statutory premise that the $528,560.00 SDTC funding was "government assistance" within the meaning of subsection 127(9) of the Act that the Appellant received, was entitled to receive or could reasonably be expected to receive in its 2014 taxation year. Due to the Minister's inclusion of the $528,560.00 in the 2014 taxation year, the Appellant's allowable SR&ED expenditures for 2014 were reduced pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Act, a recapture of SR&ED expenditures of $188,704.00 was assessed, total adjustments of $494,066.00 were made to its net income, and an ITC of $108,657.00 was denied (an amount the Court noted should actually be $102,497.00, because non-government assistance of $17,600.00 had not been considered in calculating qualified expenditures), resulting in tax payable of $67,907.00, a repeat late-filing penalty of $13,581.40, and accrued interest; subsequently, on August 22, 2016, the Minister reassessed the 2014 taxation year at the Appellant's request to give effect to a $240,686.00 non-capital loss carryback from the 2015 taxation year, reducing the assessed tax payable from $67,907.00 to $37,989.00, while the late-filing penalty remained the same.
Governing Statutory Framework

The legal dispute in Borealis Geopower operates at the intersection of five core statutory mechanisms within the Canadian Income Tax Act governing funded research, expenditure pool deductions, tax credit computation, and collection enforcement.

First, subsection 248(1) of the Act establishes the foundational technical definition of "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Although the Minister audited and accepted that the Appellant's geothermal exploration and development activities satisfied subsection 248(1), this provision remains the statutory gateway through which expenditures enter the section 37 pool and qualify for section 127 credits.

Second, paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Act governs the mandatory reduction of a taxpayer's cumulative SR&ED expenditure pool. Under paragraph 37(1)(d), the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada must be reduced by the total of all amounts of government assistance or non-government assistance (as defined in subsection 127(9)) in respect of SR&ED that the taxpayer "has received, is entitled to receive or can reasonably be expected to receive" at or before the filing-due date for the taxation year. This statutory formula intentionally prevents taxpayers from claiming both non-taxable or deferred public subsidies and full tax deductions on the same underlying research expenditure base.

Third, subsection 127(9) of the Act defines "government assistance" broadly as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or as any other form of assistance—excluding only the federal SR&ED ITC itself. Under subsection 127(18) of the Act, any amount of government assistance that reduces the section 37 expenditure pool simultaneously reduces the taxpayer's "qualified expenditures" eligible for SR&ED ITCs on a dollar-for-dollar basis.

Fourth, where the government assistance and other amounts deducted under paragraph 37(1)(d) exceed the taxpayer's SR&ED expenditures, the excess is included in income under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the Act—an outcome the decision describes as a "recapture of SR&ED expenditures"—while the same assistance also reduces, under subsection 127(18), the qualified expenditures on which the SR&ED ITC is computed. When the Minister included the $528,560.00 SDTC advance in the Appellant's 2014 taxation year, the resulting reduction in allowable SR&ED expenditures triggered a recapture of SR&ED expenditures of $188,704.00 and the denial of the ITC, creating Part I tax payable of $67,907.00 for 2014 (later reduced to $37,989.00 by the loss carryback reassessment).

Fifth, section 160 of the Act functions as an anti-avoidance collection rule imposing joint and several liability on a transferee when property is transferred between non-arm's length persons for less than fair market value consideration at a time when the transferor is liable to pay tax in respect of the year of transfer or any preceding taxation year. Within Borealis Geopower, section 160 jurisprudence was addressed at paragraph 23 of the decision, where the Court relied by analogy on The Queen v. Livingston, 2008 FCA 89—which held that a deposit of funds into another person's account constitutes a transfer of property—to conclude that if funds deposited into an account constitute a "transfer," they equally constitute a "receipt" of those funds. Moreover, subsequent Canadian tax commentary has characterized the Court's ruling in Borealis Geopower as expanding exposure under section 160 on the basis that a deposit received for future work and held in a self-controlled trust account constituted a transfer for less than fair market value consideration; however, the decision itself contains no such holding, since no section 160 assessment was at issue and the Court made no finding on fair market value consideration, using Livingston solely to interpret the word "receive" in paragraph 37(1)(d).
The Court's Final Holding

Justice Campbell dismissed, without costs, the Appellant's appeal of the August 12, 2016 assessment and the August 22, 2016 reassessment for the 2014 taxation year, upholding the late-filing penalty and interest assessed by the Minister. The Tax Court of Canada noted that whether the $528,560.00 payment from SDTC was "government assistance" pursuant to subsection 127(9) of the Act was not in issue, as the Appellant's counsel had never argued that the SDTC funds were anything but government assistance. Furthermore, the Court ruled that the Appellant "received" the $528,560.00 in the 2014 taxation year within the ordinary dictionary and legal meaning of the word "received" under paragraph 37(1)(d). Because no trust agreement existed between SDTC and the Appellant, and because the Appellant had sole access to, and exercised control over, the funds in the CIBC account into which the cheque was deposited, the voluntary placement of the funds into a self-styled "trust account" did not prevent their receipt in 2014. Consequently, the Minister properly applied the $528,560.00 to reduce the Appellant's 2014 SR&ED expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(d), properly reduced its allowable SR&ED expenditures, and validly assessed the recapture of SR&ED expenditures; the Court further held that the late-filing penalty and interest were correctly calculated without regard to the 2015 non-capital loss carryback, pursuant to subsections 162(11) and 161(7) of the Act.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of the Appellant's 2014 SR&ED tax position in Borealis Geopower did not arise from a failure of geothermal science or engineering, as the Minister audited and accepted the technical eligibility of the SR&ED expenditures. Rather, the loss stemmed from a series of fatal legal, contractual, banking, and procedural deficiencies governing how government funding interacts with the SR&ED expenditure pool. A rigorous legal examination of Justice Campbell's Reasons for Judgment identifies five interconnected failures that invalidated the taxpayer's position.
1. Misinterpretation of the Statutory Triggers in Paragraph 37(1)(d) and the Ordinary Meaning of "Received"

The primary legal error committed by the Appellant was its position that funds it had voluntarily deposited into a self-designated trust account, and that remained subject to an unfulfilled condition under the Contribution Agreement, had not been "received" for purposes of paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Act. Under financial accounting standards, an advance grant or deposit received prior to the performance of the underlying work is often recorded as a deferred liability on the balance sheet and recognized in income only as the matching project expenses are incurred. However, paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Act overrides accounting deferral by mandating an immediate deduction from the SR&ED expenditure pool for any government assistance that the taxpayer "has received, is entitled to receive or can reasonably be expected to receive" at its filing-due date for the taxation year.

In evaluating whether the Appellant had "received" the $528,560.00 in 2014, Justice Campbell examined the word "received" beginning at paragraph 17 and continuing through paragraph 28 of the Reasons for Judgment. Relying on the ordinary dictionary meaning of the term as set out in several leading dictionaries and Black's Law Dictionary, including the Collins English Dictionary online—which defines "receive" as "to take (something offered) into one's hand or possession" and "to accept delivery or transmission of"—the Court drew on Canadian tax jurisprudence (Morin, Jones, Simser and Mbarga) holding that one need not actually receive the money in one's hand, "but it is sufficient that he received moneys' worth and that he derived benefits from something or he enjoyed its advantages," and that receipt includes constructive receipt. When the Appellant accepted delivery of the $528,560.00 cheque from SDTC in 2014 and deposited that cheque into its CIBC account, it took the funds into its possession. Because the Court concluded that the Appellant had actually received the funds in 2014, it did not need to rely on the alternative statutory prongs of amounts the Appellant "is entitled to receive or can reasonably be expected to receive" under paragraph 37(1)(d).
2. Failure to Establish a Valid Express Trust and Unilateral Dominion Over the CIBC Account

The central evidentiary pillar of the Appellant's case—advanced through the oral testimony of its current Chairman, Mr. Timothy Thompson—was that the $528,560.00 was not received in 2014 because the cheque was deposited into a CIBC trust account established for that purpose, where the funds were left "until such a time as we were allowed to withdraw". Under Canadian law, however, a taxpayer cannot create a valid trust relationship that binds the Minister of National Revenue merely by opening a bank account labelled "trust account" or by harbouring a subjective internal intention to restrict the use of funds. Establishing a valid express trust requires clear documentary proof of the three certainties—certainty of intention, certainty of subject matter, and certainty of objects—supported by an enforceable legal obligation that deprives the account holder of autonomous beneficial ownership and control.

At paragraphs 25 through 28 of the judgment, Justice Campbell rejected the Appellant's trust argument on the evidentiary record. First, the Court found as a fact that there was no trust agreement between SDTC and the Appellant, and that the Contribution Agreement (entered into evidence as Exhibit A-1) was silent in respect of advances deposited to a trust account set up by an eligible recipient; although there may have been an informal agreement respecting the funds, SDTC placed no formal restrictions on their use until its letter of September 16, 2016 (Exhibit A-3). Second, the Court noted that the funds were voluntarily deposited by the Appellant into the CIBC trust account rather than pursuant to any legal mandate from the grantor. Third, the trial transcript (including testimony at pages 38, 40 and 48) demonstrated that although the Appellant held the funds in an account designated as a trust account, the Appellant had sole access to the funds in that CIBC account and exercised control over them. The Appellant had the authority to deposit and withdraw, was under no obligation to notify SDTC when it transferred amounts from the trust account to another account (notifying SDTC only occasionally, upon request, of the balance), made withdrawals as the work continued, and redeposited some money at year end because of overdraws. Because the Appellant exercised control over the deposited funds—deciding, in relation to expenditures on the work project, when to withdraw and how much to withdraw—the self-imposed trust designation did not prevent receipt of the funds in 2014.
3. Conflation of Contractual Conditions Precedent with Post-Receipt Performance Covenants

The Appellant also relied on the contractual architecture of the Contribution Agreement (specifically Schedule C.3, Schedule of Payments, at page 43, and the payment conditions in paragraph 3.5) to argue that, since not all of the conditions for receipt of the funds from SDTC had been satisfied, the funds could not have been "received" in 2014. Justice Campbell reviewed the Contribution Agreement between SDTC and the Appellant, which set out the terms and conditions respecting the project and governed the obligation of SDTC to make an instalment payment.

The Court found that the Appellant's contractual interpretation could not defeat receipt: under Schedule C.3, the first advance of $528,560.83 was payable upon (1) execution of the Contribution Agreement and (2) evidence satisfactory to SDTC that Enbridge had submitted its criteria for proceeding with Phase 2 activities, and although the second condition was never fulfilled (Enbridge decided not to proceed in late 2014), SDTC proceeded with the disbursement of the instalment in 2014 regardless. Because paragraph 3.5 of the Contribution Agreement made SDTC's obligation to pay an instalment subject to the fulfillment, or the waiver by SDTC in its sole discretion, of the stated conditions, SDTC could advance an instalment before the Milestone objective was completed, and the Agreement was silent respecting Milestone achievements once such an advance was made. The Court found that the advance was given prior to the completion of the first Milestone and that no conditions were superimposed on the transfer. Accordingly, under paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Act, the unfulfilled condition precedent in the Contribution Agreement did not negate the fact that the Appellant received government assistance in the year it accepted delivery of the cheque.
4. Inapplicability of Section 160 Jurisprudence and Collateral Exposure for Corporate Transfers

During the litigation, the Appellant's counsel argued that the case law interpreting the word "receive" (discussed at paragraphs 19 to 23 of the decision, including the reasoning in Jones quoted at paragraph 21), much of it concerning bursary awards, could be distinguished because it dealt with different types of transfers than the payment of government assistance from SDTC to the Appellant, and because the Contribution Agreement outlined contractual conditions governing the spending of those funds. Justice Campbell held that, although those decisions are factually different, they provide guidance on how the Court has treated the meaning of "receive," and at paragraph 23 she relied on the section 160 decision in Livingston, 2008 FCA 89, by analogy, reasoning that if funds deposited into an individual's bank account constitute a "transfer" under section 160, they would similarly constitute a "receipt" of those funds for purposes of paragraph 37(1)(d).

Canadian tax commentators have subsequently linked Justice Campbell's determination regarding the Appellant's control over the CIBC deposit account to increased assessment exposure under section 160 of the Act. Specifically, that commentary describes Borealis Geopower as holding that a deposit received for work to be completed in the future constituted a transfer for less than fair market value consideration because the taxpayer had complete control over the account in which the deposit was held; however, the decision contains no such holding, as it concerned only the timing of receipt of government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d), no section 160 assessment was before the Court, and the Court made no finding regarding fair market value consideration. Independently of the decision, as a general matter under section 160(1), where a corporation owes corporate income tax—such as a tax debt created by an SR&ED recapture reassessment—and transfers property to a non-arm's length entity or a non-arm's length corporate director for less than fair market value consideration, the CRA may hold the transferee jointly and severally liable for the corporation's unpaid tax, up to the value of the property transferred in excess of any consideration given.
5. Procedural Late-Filing Deficiencies and Asynchronous SR&ED Recapture Mechanics

A secondary compliance issue documented by Justice Campbell at paragraphs 5, 13, and 29 of the Reasons for Judgment concerned the Appellant's repeated failure to file its corporate income tax returns within the statutory deadlines prescribed by the Act. Specifically, the Appellant's T2 returns for the 2011 and 2013 taxation years were due on July 3, 2012, and July 2, 2014, respectively, but were not filed until June 30, 2015, and its 2014 return, due on July 2, 2015, was late-filed on December 23, 2015.

This procedural non-compliance interacted with the Minister's determination of the taxation year in which the Appellant received its government funding. Because the Appellant received the $528,560.00 SDTC cheque in 2014, the Minister's inclusion of the $528,560.00 in the 2014 taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(d) applied the government assistance against the Appellant's accepted 2014 SR&ED expenditures of approximately $373,000.00. As a result, the $528,560.00 assistance reduced the Appellant's allowable 2014 SR&ED expenditures, triggering a recapture of SR&ED expenditures of $188,704.00 and the denial of the SR&ED ITC. Whereas the Appellant had originally calculated zero tax owing for 2014 on the strength of its unreduced SR&ED tax credits, the assessment created Part I tax payable of $67,907.00 for 2014, later reduced to $37,989.00 by the reassessment giving effect to the 2015 non-capital loss carryback. Once a positive tax liability existed for 2014, the Appellant's late filing on December 23, 2015—five months beyond its July 2, 2015 filing-due date and following its prior late filings for 2011 and 2013—exposed the corporation to a repeat late-filing penalty of $13,581.40 under subsection 162(2) and to arrears interest, and the Court held that, under subsections 162(11) and 161(7), neither the penalty nor the interest could be reduced by the $240,686.00 non-capital loss carryback or any ITC carryback from 2015 (Zandi v The Queen, 2012 TCC 259; Connaught Laboratories Ltd. v The Queen, 94 DTC 6697).
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and legal requirement analyzed in Borealis Geopower Inc. v. The Queen (2018 TCC 189) against the taxpayer's specific legal or evidentiary failure and the governing standard of proof articulated by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Governing Provision of the Income Tax Act (Canada)
The Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof & Holding

cells: Characterization of Public Funding as Government Assistance
Subsection 127(9) and Paragraph 37(1)(d)

Did not dispute that the $528,560.00 SDTC advance was government assistance; it argued only that the advance had not been received in 2014 because it was held in a trust account subject to unfulfilled conditions.

Not in issue: the Appellant's counsel confirmed she had never argued that the SDTC funds were anything but "government assistance" under subsection 127(9), so the Court made no ruling on characterization.
Timing of Assistance Reduction ("Received, Entitled to Receive, or Reasonably Expected")
Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(9)
Excluded the $528,560.00 SDTC advance from its 2014 return on the basis that the funds were held in a trust account and the Contribution Agreement conditions had not been met.

"Received" bears its ordinary dictionary and legal meaning: taking into one's possession or accepting delivery of moneys. Receipt occurred in 2014 when the Appellant accepted delivery of the SDTC cheque and deposited it, even though a condition precedent under the Contribution Agreement remained unfulfilled.
Establishment of a Valid Express Trust over Advance Funds
Paragraph 37(1)(d) (ordinary meaning of "receive") / Contribution Agreement (Exhibit A-1)
Voluntarily deposited the SDTC cheque into a self-styled CIBC "trust account" and relied on oral testimony of corporate intent without any formal trust agreement.

No trust agreement existed between SDTC and the Appellant, the Contribution Agreement was silent on advances deposited to a recipient's trust account, and SDTC imposed no formal restrictions until September 16, 2016; the self-designated trust account therefore did not prevent receipt (the Court did not apply a three-certainties analysis).
Restriction on Beneficial Dominion and Bank Account Control
Paragraph 37(1)(d) / Section 160 Jurisprudence (Livingston, 2008 FCA 89) applied by analogy

Had sole access to the CIBC trust account with authority to deposit and withdraw, withdrew funds as the work continued, redeposited some money at year end because of overdraws, and had no obligation to notify SDTC of transfers.

Where the taxpayer exercises control over the funds in a designated trust account—deciding when and how much to withdraw—the funds are received; by analogy to Livingston, a deposit into one's account that would be a "transfer" is equally a "receipt".
Contractual Conditions Precedent vs. Post-Receipt Covenants
Contract Law / Exhibit A-1 (SDTC Contribution Agreement)
Argued that because the Schedule C.3 condition (evidence that Enbridge had submitted its Phase 2 criteria) was never fulfilled, the advance could not have been received in 2014.

Under paragraph 3.5 of the Contribution Agreement, SDTC could require fulfillment of, or waive in its sole discretion, the payment conditions and could advance an instalment before the Milestone was completed. Because the advance was given with no conditions superimposed on the transfer, the unfulfilled condition did not negate receipt in 2014.
Calculation of Net SR&ED Pool, Recapture of SR&ED Expenditures and ITC Denial
Paragraph 37(1)(d), Subsection 127(9), and Paragraph 12(1)(v)
Calculated its 2014 SR&ED ITC without deducting the $528,560.00 SDTC advance received in 2014, reporting nil tax owing for 2014.

Government assistance received in the taxation year must reduce the section 37 SR&ED pool in that exact year. The inclusion produced a recapture of SR&ED expenditures of $188,704.00, denial of the ITC ($108,657.00 as assessed; $102,497.00 per the Court), and tax payable of $67,907.00, reduced to $37,989.00 after the 2015 loss carryback.
Use of Non-Arm's Length Transfer (Section 160) Jurisprudence by Analogy
Section 160(1) (by analogy) and Paragraph 37(1)(d)

Argued that case law interpreting "receive" (mainly bursary award cases) was distinguishable because it involved different types of transfers than government assistance subject to contractual spending conditions.

Although factually different, such cases guide the meaning of "receive"; relying on Livingston (a section 160 case), the Court held that a deposit that constitutes a "transfer" equally constitutes a "receipt" under paragraph 37(1)(d). The Court made no finding that a deposit for future work is a transfer for less than fair market value consideration under section 160, although later commentary has characterized the case that way.
Timely Filing of Corporate Tax and SR&ED Returns
Section 150; Subsections 162(2), 162(11), and 161(7)
Late-filed the 2014 corporate tax return on December 23, 2015 (due July 2, 2015), after filing its 2011 and 2013 returns late on June 30, 2015.

A repeat late-filing penalty of $13,581.40 under subsection 162(2) (five months late) and interest were upheld; under subsections 162(11) and 161(7), tax payable for penalty and interest purposes is determined without the 2015 non-capital loss carryback or ITC carryback.
Technical Eligibility of Underlying R&D Activities
Subsection 248(1) ("SR&ED")
Satisfied during audit review (the Minister accepted the underlying SR&ED expenditures, demonstrating that technical eligibility alone cannot save a flawed financial claim).

Even where the Minister accepts that the project meets the SR&ED definition under subsection 248(1) and accepts the claimed expenditures (approximately $373,000.00), the financial claim will be neutralized if government assistance received in the year is not deducted under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9).

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the legal holdings of Borealis Geopower Inc. v. The Queen (2018 TCC 189) into comprehensive compliance protocols for Canadian corporate taxpayers, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic R&D projects confronting the exact statutory, contractual, and evidentiary pitfalls identified by Justice Campbell. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how a Canadian corporation can restructure its project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, banking architecture, and experimentation tracking to overcome the Court's objections and satisfy all statutory requirements of the Canadian SR&ED regime.
Case Study 1: Clean-Tech Closed-Loop Geothermal Drilling & Supercritical Fluid Extraction System
Scenario and Pitfall Alignment

TerraTherm Clean Energy Corp. ("TerraTherm"), a privately owned Canadian-controlled private corporation ("CCPC") headquartered in Calgary, Alberta, with a December 31 fiscal year-end, is developing an experimental closed-loop deep geothermal heat exchange system in western Canada. To co-fund its field validation program, TerraTherm secures a $1,200,000 non-repayable contribution from a federal clean-technology funding foundation analogous to SDTC. Under the draft Contribution Agreement, the funding agency proposes to issue an upfront advance instalment cheque of $450,000 on November 15, 2026 (Fiscal Year 1), to fund specialized supercritical downhole drilling experiments scheduled to occur between February and August 2027 (Fiscal Year 2).

During Fiscal Year 1 (2026), TerraTherm has incurred $400,000 of eligible SR&ED salaries and Canadian subcontractor expenditures on preliminary reservoir simulation and metallurgical testing, expecting to claim a 35% enhanced refundable federal SR&ED ITC ($140,000) plus Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant to offset its corporate tax payable. TerraTherm's Chief Financial Officer proposes depositing the $450,000 advance cheque into a segregated CIBC corporate bank account internally designated as the "TerraTherm Project Trust Account" in November 2026, intending to exclude the $450,000 from TerraTherm's 2026 Schedule T2SCH31 and Form T661 filings and report the assistance in 2027 as the funds are transferred into the general operating account to pay drilling subcontractors.

Applying the reasoning in Borealis Geopower, this unmediated arrangement will trigger an immediate tax reassessment. Upon audit, the CRA will determine that the $450,000 payment constitutes "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and was "received" by TerraTherm in 2026 under paragraph 37(1)(d) the moment the cheque was deposited into the CIBC account over which TerraTherm exercises unilateral control. The inclusion of the $450,000 in 2026 will reduce TerraTherm's $400,000 SR&ED expenditure pool for 2026 to zero, eliminate its $140,000 refundable ITC, and trigger an SR&ED recapture assessment on the $50,000 excess assistance against prior pool claims. Furthermore, if TerraTherm transfers any portion of the unspent deposit to a related holding company or director prior to completing the work, the CRA will have grounds to issue a derivative assessment under section 160(1).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring of the Contribution Agreement Terms

To prevent paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Act from capturing the $450,000 in Fiscal Year 1 (2026) under any of its three statutory triggers—"has received, is entitled to receive or can reasonably be expected to receive"—TerraTherm's tax counsel must renegotiate and redraft the payment and scope mechanics of the Contribution Agreement prior to execution. First, counsel must convert the disbursement schedule from an advance-instalment model to an arrears-reimbursement milestone model, or contractually schedule the Phase 2 drilling advance so that neither disbursement nor invoice submission can occur prior to July 1, 2027, after TerraTherm's June 30, 2027 filing-due date for Fiscal Year 1 (2026).

Second, to ensure the $450,000 is not swept into 2026 as an amount TerraTherm "is entitled to receive or can reasonably be expected to receive" as of its June 30, 2027 filing-due date for Fiscal Year 1, the Contribution Agreement must embed genuine, substantive conditions precedent to entitlement that cannot be satisfied until 2027. Specifically, the payment clause must stipulate that the funding agency has zero legal obligation to disburse the $450,000 Phase 2 tranche unless and until: (a) TerraTherm's Phase 1 autoclave metallurgical corrosion trials achieve a verified pressure-integrity benchmark certified by an independent third-party petroleum engineering firm on or after July 10, 2027; and (b) the provincial energy regulator accepts TerraTherm's post-drilling well-integrity report for the experimental deep-well thermal injection program in Q3 2027. Because the satisfaction of both technical certification and regulatory acceptance remains genuinely uncertain at TerraTherm's June 30, 2027 filing-due date, TerraTherm is neither entitled to receive nor can reasonably be expected to receive the Phase 2 tranche in 2026 under paragraph 37(1)(d).

Third, because paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9) only require the deduction of government assistance received in respect of SR&ED, counsel must incorporate an explicit Contractual Cost-Category Allocation Schedule inside the Contribution Agreement. Clean-technology field pilots routinely encompass both eligible SR&ED activities (experimental downhole heat-exchanger testing) and ineligible commercial or capital infrastructure activities (access road grading, environmental baseline assessments, surface civil works, and commercial grid interconnection). By contractually binding specific funding tranches exclusively to non-SR&ED infrastructure budget lines and prohibiting the reallocation of those funds to SR&ED wages or subcontractors, TerraTherm legally insulates its SR&ED expenditure pool from reduction by the non-SR&ED portion of the grant.
Step 2: Independent Tripartite Escrow and Trust Architecture

In instances where the public funding agency's parliamentary appropriation requires it to disburse the $450,000 out of its fiscal budget before December 31, 2026, TerraTherm must directly cure the evidentiary defects identified by Justice Campbell in Borealis Geopower—namely, that there was "no trust agreement between SDTC and the Appellant," that the deposit into CIBC was voluntary, and that the Appellant retained complete control over the bank account.

Rather than accepting a cheque payable to TerraTherm and depositing it into a corporate CIBC account, TerraTherm, the Funding Agency, and an independent federally regulated Canadian trust company (acting as Escrow Trustee) must execute a formal Tripartite Escrow Trust Deed prior to any disbursement. Under the terms of the Trust Deed, the Funding Agency wires the $450,000 directly to the Escrow Trustee's statutory trust account. The Trust Deed must satisfy the three certainties of trust law by explicitly stating that the Escrow Trustee holds the funds in trust for the sole benefit of the Funding Agency (as Settlor and primary Beneficiary) until specified 2027 technical conditions precedent are certified in writing by the Funding Agency. Crucially, TerraTherm must have zero signatory authority over the escrow account, zero unilateral right to instruct the bank or trustee to release funds, and zero ability to pledge or assign the escrowed funds as security to creditors. Any interest earned on the escrow balance in 2026 must accrue legally to the Funding Agency. By completely divesting TerraTherm of possession, dominion, and control in 2026, the corporation does not "receive" the funds in 2026 under the dictionary or legal test applied in Borealis Geopower.
Step 3: Project Governance and Corporate Tax Compliance Controls

To eliminate general section 160 risks and the procedural late-filing penalties highlighted in Borealis Geopower, TerraTherm's board of directors must institute a binding Corporate Tax and SR&ED Governance Charter. First, the charter must mandate a strict tax compliance calendar requiring the completion of annual financial audits, Form T661 technical narratives, and Schedule T2SCH31 pool calculations within 120 days of the December 31 fiscal year-end, ensuring that the T2 corporate income tax return is filed well before the June 30 statutory filing due date under section 150 of the Act. Timely filing eliminates late-filing penalties and ensures that even if an audit adjustment alters the SR&ED pool, the corporation is never exposed to compounding procedural penalties.

Second, the Governance Charter must establish a strict Section 160 Intercompany Transfer Protocol. Under this protocol, TerraTherm is prohibited from paying dividends, redeeming shares, reimbursing unvouchered personal travel expenses, or advancing funds to directors, shareholders, or non-arm's length affiliates unless two conditions are met: (a) a formal solvency and tax-provision review confirms nil Part I tax and nil SR&ED recapture exposure; and (b) every intercompany or director payment is executed strictly in exchange for simultaneous, documented fair market value consideration (such as settled T4 employment remuneration or completed engineering services rather than deposits for future work), completely insulating corporate directors from personal liability under section 160(1).
Step 4: Technical Documentation and Experimentation Tracking Protocols

To maintain the high standard of technical eligibility under subsection 248(1) that Borealis Geopower achieved on audit, while proving the financial separation between funded and unfunded project phases, TerraTherm must implement a rigorous Contemporaneous Experimentation and Cost-Segregation System. In geothermal exploration and development, CRA Research and Technology Advisors routinely scrutinize whether field activities are merely standard geological prospecting (characterizing local rock formations using established drilling techniques) or genuine SR&ED aimed at resolving a fundamental technological uncertainty.

TerraTherm's technical documentation must explicitly isolate routine geological mapping from its core technological uncertainty: whether a novel silicon-carbide-doped polymer grout and coaxial titanium liner can maintain structural bond integrity and thermal conductivity above 2.0 W/(m·K) when subjected to cyclic supercritical thermal shock (25°C to 400°C) and hypersaline sour brine corrosion without micro-annulus delamination. Every experimental iteration must be logged contemporaneously in an immutable electronic engineering ledger containing a dated hypothesis, quantitative boundary conditions, downhole fibre-optic distributed temperature sensing (DTS) logs, ultrasonic cement bond logs, and failure-mode analyses. Simultaneously, TerraTherm's accounting general ledger must assign distinct cost-centre tracking codes to each work package—specifically segregating Unfunded SR&ED Experiments (Cost Centre 100), Grant-Co-Funded SR&ED Experiments (Cost Centre 200), and Grant-Funded Non-SR&ED Civil/Commercial Infrastructure (Cost Centre 300)—requiring all employee timesheets and subcontractor invoices to reference both the technical experiment ID and the dedicated financial cost centre.
Case Study 2: Industrial AI Predictive Grid-Balancing Software and Public Authority Contract Structuring
Scenario and Pitfall Alignment

VoltGrid Analytics Inc. ("VoltGrid"), an Ontario-based CCPC with a June 30 fiscal year-end, develops real-time machine-learning algorithms for autonomous load-balancing and harmonic stabilization across distributed renewable microgrids. In May 2026 (one month prior to its June 30, 2026 fiscal year-end), VoltGrid enters into two separate funding arrangements:

items: A Provincial Clean-Tech Grant Agreement with a provincial government innovation agency providing $300,000 in non-repayable grant assistance, under which an initial $180,000 advance cheque is received on June 10, 2026, and deposited by VoltGrid into a secondary chartered bank account designated on its internal chart of accounts as a "Restricted Grant Trust Account".

A Pilot Deployment Agreement with a provincial Crown hydro utility (a public authority), under which the utility pays VoltGrid a $250,000 upfront deposit on June 15, 2026, for custom software adaptation and microgrid telemetry integration to be executed between July 2026 and March 2027 (Fiscal Year 2027).

body.text: VoltGrid's management assumes that neither the $180,000 provincial grant advance nor the $250,000 Crown utility deposit will reduce its FY2026 SR&ED expenditure pool of $420,000 because both payments sit in the internal "Restricted Grant Trust Account" awaiting FY2027 project execution. Furthermore, in late June 2026, VoltGrid transfers $200,000 from that bank account to its founder and sole director as an unscheduled shareholder draw while delaying the filing of its FY2026 corporate tax return until November 2027.

Under Borealis Geopower, VoltGrid faces severe multi-front reassessment exposure. First, the $180,000 provincial grant advance deposited on June 10, 2026, into a company-controlled bank account will be ruled "received" in FY2026 under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9). Second, because the provincial hydro utility is a public authority, the $250,000 upfront deposit will be assessed by the CRA as either "government assistance" or a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) received in FY2026, wiping out the remaining $240,000 of VoltGrid's FY2026 SR&ED pool and triggering SR&ED recapture on the $10,000 excess. Third, because the $200,000 transfer to the founder-director (a non-arm's length person) occurred for no fair market value consideration while VoltGrid owed corporate tax for FY2026, the CRA can assess the founder-director personally under section 160(1) for the corporation's unpaid tax and late-filing penalties.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring of the Crown Utility Agreement and Provincial Grant Timing

To prevent the $250,000 Crown utility agreement from disqualifying VoltGrid's SR&ED expenditure pool as either "government assistance" or a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d), tax counsel must fundamentally restructure the commercial contract prior to execution. Under subsection 127(9) of the Act, an amount paid by a Canadian customer or public authority constitutes a disqualifying "contract payment" only if it is payable for SR&ED to be performed for or on behalf of that payer. Counsel must redraft the utility agreement as a standard Commercial Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) Subscription and API Access Agreement rather than a custom R&D development contract. The contract terms must explicitly stipulate that: (a) the utility is purchasing a commercial right to access output load-balancing predictions from VoltGrid's proprietary platform; (b) the utility is not contracting for, directing, or funding scientific research; (c) 100% of all underlying intellectual property, source code, and algorithmic weights remain the exclusive property of VoltGrid; and (d) VoltGrid bears complete financial and technical risk if its internal R&D fails to meet latency specifications.

Simultaneously, to eliminate the receipt-timing exposure that was decisive in Borealis Geopower, counsel must synchronize the payment mechanics of both the Commercial SaaS Agreement and the Provincial Clean-Tech Grant Agreement with VoltGrid's fiscal calendar and its December 31, 2026 filing-due date for FY2026. Specifically, both agreements must eliminate the June 2026 upfront deposits and set the earliest contractual invoicing and disbursement date as January 5, 2027 (Fiscal Year 2027), contingent upon VoltGrid delivering its formal Interim Architecture Milestone Report on or after January 2, 2027. By legally deferring both entitlement and physical receipt of the $180,000 provincial grant until January 2027, after the FY2026 filing-due date, the paragraph 37(1)(d) government assistance deduction occurs in FY2027—the exact taxation year in which VoltGrid incurs the matching $500,000 of FY2027 software engineering salaries—preserving 100% of VoltGrid's $420,000 FY2026 SR&ED expenditure pool intact.
Step 2: Dismantling Self-Styled Internal Trust Accounts and Implementing True Banking Segregation

VoltGrid must immediately abandon the practice of depositing incoming grants or customer advances into a company-controlled bank account labelled "Restricted Grant Trust Account" on its internal balance sheet. As Justice Campbell established in Borealis Geopower, a recipient's sole access to and control over funds in a self-designated trust account means the trust label does not prevent receipt for purposes of paragraph 37(1)(d). Where a commercial customer or public agency insists on lodging a financial security deposit before July 1, 2026, to guarantee project capacity, the deposit must be placed with an arm's length commercial escrow agent or law firm trust account under a written Escrow Deposit Agreement stipulating that the funds remain the beneficial property of the customer until released upon delivery of verified commercial software milestones in FY2027, with VoltGrid barred from exercising any signatory control or borrowing power against the account prior to release.
Step 3: Project Governance to Neutralize Section 160 Director Liability and Late-Filing Recapture

To protect VoltGrid's founder-director from personal liability under section 160(1) and shield the corporation from SR&ED recapture and late-filing penalties, VoltGrid must restructure its executive compensation and tax filing governance. Under Canadian section 160 jurisprudence, transferring $200,000 to a non-arm's length director via a shareholder draw or dividend provides zero fair market value consideration to the corporation, automatically exposing the director to joint and several liability up to the transferred amount for any corporate tax debt owing in respect of FY2026 or prior years. Instead, VoltGrid must execute a formal Executive Employment and R&D Supervision Agreement with its founder-director, paying all compensation as regular T4 employment salary in exchange for documented, contemporaneous engineering and corporate management services. Not only does remuneration for actual services rendered constitute fair market value consideration that defeats a section 160 assessment, but the portion of the founder-director's salary directly attributable to hands-on participation in eligible SR&ED experimentation (up to the statutory proxy limits for specified employees) also qualifies as an eligible SR&ED expenditure under section 37.

Furthermore, VoltGrid's corporate governance policy must mandate a Pre-Filing SR&ED Pool & Recapture Audit 60 days prior to the statutory T2 filing deadline (December 31, 2026, for a June 30 year-end). This internal review verifies all assistance received or receivable by the filing-due date under paragraph 37(1)(d), models any potential section 127 recapture, and guarantees timely electronic transmission of the T2 return, Form T661, and Schedule T2SCH31.
Step 4: Software Experimentation Tracking and Technical Documentation

To substantiate that VoltGrid's underlying algorithm development meets the strict requirements of subsection 248(1) of the Act and remains distinct from routine commercial telemetry integration performed for the hydro utility, VoltGrid must enforce a structured Hypothesis-Driven Software Engineering Protocol. In software SR&ED audits, the CRA requires clear proof of technological uncertainty—demonstrating that standard mathematical models, publicly available machine-learning frameworks, and known software engineering architectures could not achieve the required computational objectives due to fundamental system constraints.

VoltGrid must configure its version-control (Git) and project-management (Jira) architecture so that all SR&ED work is tracked within dedicated experimental repositories separated from commercial client-integration branches. Each experimental sprint must open with a formal Technical Uncertainty & Hypothesis Record documenting the exact system-level bottleneck (for example, why existing recurrent neural networks fail to achieve sub-10-millisecond convergence under non-stationary inverter phase shifts without numerical instability). Every code commit and automated test run must log quantitative performance metrics (convergence latency distributions, memory allocation ceilings, and harmonic distortion residuals) alongside a dated engineering analysis explaining why the tested algorithmic modification succeeded or failed. Developer timesheets must be recorded daily against specific experimental ticket IDs, providing a seamless, contemporaneous evidentiary bridge between the technical investigation under subsection 248(1) and the financial expenditure pools calculated under section 37 and subsection 127(9).

body.text: 5. Strategic Conclusions for Canadian Tax Advisors

The ruling of the Tax Court of Canada in Borealis Geopower Inc. v. The Queen, 2018 TCC 189, serves as an essential cautionary example (though, as an informal procedure decision, not a binding precedent) for Canadian corporations and their legal and technical tax advisors. As the decision demonstrates, satisfying the scientific and engineering criteria of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act during a CRA technical review provides no fiscal protection if the taxpayer mismanages the timing and characterization of government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9). When public funding is received in a taxation year—even where a condition precedent under the funding agreement remains unfulfilled and the funds sit in a self-designated trust account—paragraph 37(1)(d) operates to reduce that year's SR&ED expenditure pool and can trigger a recapture of SR&ED expenditures, the denial of ITCs, and Part I tax liability, together with late-filing penalties and interest that a later loss carryback cannot reduce.

Equally critical is the Court's uncompromising rejection of informal, self-administered trust arrangements. Merely depositing government grants or commercial advances into a chartered bank account designated as a "trust account"—while retaining unilateral control to transfer funds without an external trust agreement—will not defer statutory receipt under paragraph 37(1)(d), and, under the general rules of section 160 of the Act (which the Court invoked only by analogy to construe "receipt"), will not shield non-arm's length transferees and corporate directors from derivative tax liability on transfers of such funds for inadequate consideration. By integrating proactive tax counsel at the contract-drafting stage to align grant disbursements with fiscal year-ends, establishing independent tripartite escrow trusts where pre-funding is unavoidable, contractually segregating non-SR&ED project funding, and maintaining rigorous contemporaneous technical and financial records, Canadian innovators can fully satisfy the statutory mandate of the Income Tax Act and safeguard their SR&ED Investment Tax Credits against audit reassessment.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; court ruled the activities did not meet the statutory definition of SR&ED under the Income Tax Act.
